analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal price supports and production quotas for the US sugar industry.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase out sugar price supports and quotas died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or a vote, having drawn only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would gradually wind down the federal sugar program. It cuts the government-guaranteed minimum price for sugarcane and sugar beets a little each year, stops guaranteeing those loans after the 2004 crop, repeals the quotas that limit how much sugar growers can sell, and directs the President to make sure enough sugar reaches the US market at prices no higher than the world price or the loan rate, whichever is higher. The goal is cheaper sugar for consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: American households and businesses that buy sugar would benefit. The US sugar program keeps the domestic price of sugar above the world price through government-backed loans at a fixed rate and by restricting how much sugar can be produced and sold domestically; every food and drink containing sugar carries that higher price. The bill would lower those guaranteed loan rates each year (from 18 cents per pound for the 2001 crop down to 14 cents for the 2004 crop), make loans recourse so the government no longer takes possession of sugar when prices fall, end all price supports for the 2005 crop and later, repeal the sugar marketing quotas and acreage allotments, and direct the President to ensure adequate sugar supplies reach the US market at prices no greater than the higher of the world price or the loan rate [S3][S2]. Food and beverage manufacturers that use sugar as an input would also gain from lower ingredient costs.

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the guaranteed loan rate for raw cane sugar in steps from 18 cents per pound to 14 cents per pound by the 2004 crop, directly reducing the price floor that keeps US sugar prices high

Converts the loans from nonrecourse to recourse, so processors could no longer hand their sugar to the government when market prices fall below the loan rate; the price floor would no longer be backed by government purchases
Ends all federal price support for sugarcane and sugar beets for the 2005 crop and every crop after it
Repeals the sugar and crystalline fructose marketing quotas and acreage allotments, ending government-enforced limits on how much sugar can be produced and sold

Directs the President to use all available authority to ensure adequate raw cane sugar supplies reach the US market at prices no greater than the higher of the world price or the loan rate, addressing the concern that removing quotas could cause shortages

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and the processors who mill their crops would bear the cost. They would lose the guaranteed minimum prices (loan rates set by law at 18 cents per pound for raw cane sugar), the government's promise to take their sugar if the market price fell below that floor, and the marketing quotas and acreage allotments that guarantee them a share of the US sugar market and keep competing imports limited [S3][S2]. Regions built around sugar farming would absorb the adjustment.

drawbacks.text: The bill would expose sugar growers to world prices that are themselves pushed down by heavily subsidized foreign producers, so US growers — and the farm towns that depend on them — could face years of prices below the true cost of production
The transition is abrupt: all price support ends with the 2005 crop while loan rates are still being cut, giving growers and processors little time to adjust to a market with no floor

Losing the marketing quotas and allotments would end the guaranteed share of the market that sugar farm operations in states like Florida and Minnesota are built around, threatening farm-level income even before world competition is weighed

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but diffuse: cheaper sugar for every household and food manufacturer, paid for by a small group of growers and processors who currently enjoy one of the most protected markets in American agriculture. The bill is also honest about the transition risk — it keeps a floor (the loan rate) in place through 2004 and directs the President to maintain adequate supplies — but it offers no adjustment assistance for sugar-dependent farm communities, and growers facing a world price depressed by foreign subsidies would bear real hardship. On balance, ending a program that taxes every consumer through higher food prices to support a small, concentrated group is a net gain for the public, though a badly cushioned one for the growers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 7, 2001 by Senator Rick Santorum, joined by Senator John McCain as the only other original cosponsor
It drew one additional cosponsor — one Republican and one Democrat in total — before the Congress ended
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the day it was introduced
The action history shows no markup, no committee report, no floor action, and no vote of any kind after the referral
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill died in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar cane and beet growers and processors came out ahead: the price supports, government-backed loans, and marketing quotas that keep the domestic sugar price above the world price stayed in place for the rest of the Congress. American consumers kept paying the higher sugar prices the program produces.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers and processors, shielded from competition

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew only two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: Their revenue depends on the program this bill would phase out: government loan rates that set a floor price and marketing quotas that limit supply and restrict competition. The program's cost lands on consumers, who pay above-world prices for sugar in nearly everything they buy.
Beet sugar is covered by the same loan program and quota system. The bill would cut their guaranteed loan rate and end all price support for the 2005 crop and later, exposing them to market prices.
They buy sugar as a main ingredient at the program-inflated domestic price. Ending supports and quotas would lower their input costs, savings that would partly pass through to shoppers.
